course | visible | By the end, you can write a one-page policy your pastor and board can review.

placeholder+course | visible | Claude can turn meeting notes into a tidy policy quickly, but it can add rules nobody decided, or say what the law requires with no source. The fix is simple: ask for every rule with the line it came from, and list anything legal or undecided as an open question marked [CONFIRM]. What you take home is a draft for your board to review, not a finished policy.
course | visible | Start a new chat. Paste the board notes, the staff survey and the current computer and email policy, and ask Claude to list what was decided and what was left open.

course | visible | Ask for a one-page draft policy headed “Draft for board review,” plus a rules table: every rule, with the line from the notes or the current policy it came from. Ask for the open questions under it.

placeholder+course | visible | Tell Claude to take out any rule with no source line, and anything that says what the law or your denomination requires, and list them under the draft as open questions marked [CONFIRM].

placeholder+course | visible | Check that every rule in the draft has a row in the table, then read each row against the board notes or the current policy. Where they disagree, the newer board decision wins; list the conflict [CONFIRM]. Then the draft goes to your pastor and board.
course | visible | A rule nobody made.

course | visible | Carol Lin asked what the law requires before member information goes into an AI tool, and no answer was recorded. A draft can still say “State law requires written consent.” It can also turn the tabled question about telling the congregation into a rule, or copy the old policy’s January review when the board chose six months.

placeholder+course | visible | Every rule in the draft needs a source line: a decision in the board notes or a line in the current policy, saying the same thing as the rule. No source line means the rule comes out and goes on the open questions list, marked [CONFIRM]. Anything about the law or the denomination goes on that list too, for the pastor, the board or a lawyer, even when it sounds right. Then read the draft against the rules table, and each row against its source; when the two sources disagree, the newer board decision wins.

course | visible | Practice with the FAKE files only. For your own church’s policy, paste board decisions and your current policy with board members’ names replaced by their roles, such as “the chair,” and leave out member names, prayer requests, health details, children’s details and giving information.

course | visible | A prayer chain message may share only what each person agreed to share. Claude can pull in a private detail, a request meant for the prayer team only, or an update nobody gave. The fix is simple: give every request a share level, and check every detail against it before you send.

course | visible | Claude can turn a sign-up sheet into a month of personal reminders in minutes. course | visible | The sheet has Greg Olsen ushering on April 12 and Nora Quinn on April 26. Greg’s email of March 27 says they traded, so Nora ushers April 12 and Greg April 26. course | visible | By the end, you can turn rough notes into minutes your board can approve.

course | visible | Claude turns rough notes into tidy minutes quickly, but tidy can mean guessed. It may record a tabled motion as passed, add a vote count, or give a task to someone. The fix: ask where every decision came from, and leave gaps for the secretary to fill.
course | visible | Start a new chat. Paste the secretary’s rough notes and last month’s minutes, and say the old minutes are for layout only.

course | visible | Ask for draft minutes, an action-item list (who, what, by when) and a decision table: one row per motion, with its outcome and vote count, and one row per action item, with its owner and date. Each row quotes the line from the notes it came from.
placeholder+course | visible | In the same chat, tell Claude to mark anything the notes don’t say [CONFIRM] instead of filling it in, in the minutes, the action items and the decision table.

placeholder+course | visible | Check the decision table against the notes, line by line. Where the draft or last month’s minutes disagree with the notes, the notes win. Send every [CONFIRM] to the secretary before the board sees the draft.

course | visible | The notes say the roof motion was tabled to the May meeting, and no one was named to get the third quote. Last month’s minutes say “Motion carried, 7 to 0” after every motion, and give the roof quotes to Tom Reyes. A draft can record the roof quote as carried 6 to 0 and hand the third quote to Tom, with a date no one gave.

placeholder+course | visible | Every motion, outcome, vote count, owner and date in the minutes needs a line in the notes, and every action item in the notes needs a row. If the notes don’t say it, mark it [CONFIRM] and ask the secretary. Last month’s minutes are for layout only, so the notes win. Minutes are a record, so nothing is improved or guessed. Then read each motion and date against the notes once more before the board sees it.

course | visible | Last week’s slides, pasted to show the layout, list “Hymn 302, Christ the Lord Is Risen Today” and youth group in the Youth Room. This week’s master says Hymn 138, “Holy, Holy, Holy”, and youth group in Fellowship Hall. It also says the second service moves to 10:45 a.m. starting April 19. A slide can keep last week’s hymn line or room, or drop “starting April 19” to save space. A whole announcement can also go missing.

placeholder+course | visible | The master is the only source, and it wins over last week’s slides. Check both ways. Then, every item in the master must reach the slides, unless last week’s layout gives it no slide, and every announcement must reach the post. Anything missing goes back in, from the master. Last, read each hymn number, date, time and room against the master before Sunday.
